tldr: We propose PACE, a framework that pretrains visual and force/torque representations using proprioception (joint positions and velocities)—the most consistent signal between simulation and hardware—as an anchor, achieving a 93.3% assembly success rate without real-world fine-tuning or object tracking.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the PACE encoder. Across visual and force/torque streams, difference kernels remove static appearance and offsets, and the model predicts proprioceptive state transitions (bidirectional forward and backward) to learn essential physical motion codes shared between simulation and hardware.
overview:
Contact-rich assembly requiring submillimeter precision is one of the most challenging tasks in robot learning. While reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation is promising, there is a large sim-to-real gap across camera images, force/torque (F/T) measurements, and contact dynamics. Conventional approaches relying on object pose estimation get jammed from estimation errors of just a few millimeters, and adaptation methods using real-world data incur substantial costs.

To address this, the authors observed that proprioception (joint positions and velocities) exhibits remarkably minimal discrepancy between simulation and the real world compared to vision and force sensing. Leveraging proprioception as a shared domain anchor, they devised PACE, a method that pretrains encoders to predict subtle joint state transitions from visual and force/torque features. Because static domain-specific factors like lighting, texture, and sensor biases provide no useful information for predicting joint motion, the model naturally discards them and extracts only the motion cues required for the task.

In experiments, RL policies were trained in simulation using the frozen pretrained encoder and deployed zero-shot to a Franka Emika FR3 robot without any real-world fine-tuning. Evaluated across four assembly tasks from the Factory and AutoMate benchmarks, PACE achieved a high average real-world success rate of 93.3%, with only a 2.7-percentage-point performance drop from simulation. It also demonstrated outstanding robustness against disturbances such as lighting variations and sensor biases.
contributions: Proposed "proprioception anchoring," which uses proprioceptive state transition prediction—highly consistent between simulation and hardware—as a self-supervised signal to acquire domain-invariant visual and force/torque representations without real-world data.

Introduced a learnable zero-sum temporal difference kernel that eliminates static offsets, along with a masked reconstruction loss that prevents inter-modality redundancy and promotes complementarity.

Achieved an average zero-shot real-world success rate of 93.3% across four contact-rich assembly tasks without external pose estimators or real-world fine-tuning, with a sim-to-real drop of only 2.7 percentage points.

sections.heading: Why is Sim-to-Real So Difficult for Contact-Rich Assembly?
sections.summary: Assembly tasks with submillimeter clearances require both vision and force sensing, but discrepancies between simulation and reality pose a major hurdle. This work introduces PACE, which learns robust representations anchored by proprioception that remains consistent across domains.
sections.details:
Unlike pick-and-place tasks, contact-rich assembly demands extremely tight, submillimeter clearances (around 0.1 to 1.0 mm). Even a slight misalignment causes mating parts to jam, making high-precision spatial awareness and delicate contact force control indispensable.

Simulated reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective tool for safe, scalable data collection. However, rendered visual appearances, physical contact dynamics, and force/torque (F/T) sensor values inevitably diverge significantly from hardware. Conventional methods often estimate 3D object poses using external computer vision to feed into controllers, but errors of just a few millimeters caused by lighting changes or camera calibration drift directly lead to task failure.

Here lies the key breakthrough. While camera images and force readings drift wildly across environments, calibrated joint angles and velocities—proprioception—share the exact same physical definitions in simulation and reality. This paper establishes proprioception as a shared cross-domain anchor. By training an encoder to predict joint state transitions from temporal visual and force features, PACE naturally ignores appearance mismatches and static sensor biases, extracting only the physical motion cues needed to complete the task.

sections.heading: Limitations of Existing Approaches and Trends in Multimodal Learning
sections.summary: We compare PACE against conventional domain randomization, real-world adaptation, and existing multimodal representation learning methods. PACE stands out by capturing physical dynamics through proprioceptive supervision without requiring external pose tracking or real-world data.
sections.details:
### Contact-Rich Robotic Assembly
Classical assembly relied on compliance mechanisms or impedance control, but required custom redesigns for each part geometry. Recently, RL methods using benchmarks like Factory in Isaac Gym have gained traction, yet real-world deployments (such as IndustReal and AutoMate) still depend on external pose estimation via AprilTags or Mask R-CNN, leaving them vulnerable to perception errors. On the other hand, force-specialized approaches like FORGE excel at tactile search but lack vision, struggling during initial alignment.

### Sim-to-Real Transfer Approaches
Domain Randomization (DR) trains policies over broad parameter distributions, but residual gaps remain fatal for submillimeter tolerances. Domain Adaptation (DA) and System Identification (SysID) demand real-world data or meticulous calibration, which are costly. Asymmetric training—where a Critic accesses privileged simulation state while the Actor receives observations—is also widespread, yet transfer still collapses if observation representations diverge across domains.

### Representation Learning for Robot Manipulation
General vision models like R3M and DINOv2 do not capture the millimeter-scale geometric shifts or contact dynamics necessary for assembly. Multimodal pretraining methods like MSDP exist, but they reconstruct entire modalities using a unified transformer. PACE differs fundamentally by maintaining separate temporal difference streams for each modality and constraining representations through the explicit physical dynamics of proprioceptive transition prediction.

sections.heading: Problem Formulation: How to Define the Three Gaps
sections.summary: We formulate submillimeter assembly under operational space impedance control governing end-effector position and yaw. Among visual, force, and physical interaction gaps, proprioception serves as the sole reliable shared coordinate frame.
sections.details:
This study considers quasi-static contact-rich assembly tasks. At each step, the robot receives wrist camera images $\mathbf{I}^L_t, \mathbf{I}^R_t$, 6-axis wrist F/T readings $\mathbf{F}_t$, 7-DoF joint positions $\mathbf{q}_t$ and velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_t$, and the previous action $\mathbf{a}_{t-1}$. Actions are 4-DoF displacement commands $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, \Delta\theta_{\mathrm{yaw}})$ for end-effector position and yaw, with roll and pitch fixed vertically.

Three main gaps exist between simulation and the real world:
- Visual observation gap: Differences between rendered and real camera images.
- F/T measurement gap: Discrepancies between simulated contact models and real sensor behaviors.
- Physical interaction gap: Mismatches in friction coefficients and robot mechanical compliance.

Here, the critical assumption is proprioceptive consistency. Proprioceptive state $\mathbf{p}_t = [\mathbf{q}_t; \dot{\mathbf{q}}_t]$ is defined in identical joint coordinate systems in both simulation and the real robot, and joint velocities are derived using the same discrete-time differencing at identical control frequencies. Thus, even if visual and force distributions diverge, the proprioceptive distribution remains virtually identical across domains. If the encoder $\phi$ ties its latent features $\mathbf{z}_t$ directly to proprioception, it can acquire domain-invariant representations without requiring real-world data.

sections.heading: PACE Methodology: Zero-Sum Kernels and Proprioception Anchoring
sections.summary: We explain the pipeline from expert trajectory collection to multi-objective encoder pretraining, followed by frozen-encoder RL training and hardware deployment. Learnable zero-sum differencing and bidirectional proprioceptive prediction form the core.
sections.details:
### Expert Demonstration Collection
PPO expert policies with privileged observations (ground-truth poses and contact states) are trained in Isaac Lab. After reaching near-100% success, 300 successful trajectories per task are collected, recording camera views, wrist F/T histories, joint states, and contact flags.

### Encoder Architecture and Temporal Differencing
The encoder maintains separate streams for vision and force sensing. It buffers fixed DINOv2 features and F/T inputs over a window of $T$ steps and extracts temporal changes using 1D depthwise convolution kernels. These kernels are constrained by a zero-sum property where weights sum strictly to zero. This enforces the cancellation of static offsets like background appearances or sensor drift, preserving only pure motion codes $\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{v+}_t, \boldsymbol{\alpha}^{f+}_t$.

### Multi-Objective Dynamics Pretraining
Pretraining optimizes three objectives:
- **Proprioception Anchoring Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}$)**: Predicts the joint state change $\Delta\mathbf{p}_t = \mathbf{p}_t - \mathbf{p}_{t-K}$ from motion codes and the joint state from $K$ steps earlier $\mathbf{p}_{t-K}$. Predicting state changes rather than absolute values prevents degenerate solutions that merely copy the prior state. A cycle consistency loss also predicts past states by reversing the temporal difference.
- **Task-Relevant Auxiliary Losses**: Leveraging simulation privileges, the model learns a spatial alignment loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}$ predicting planar vectors toward target positions, and an engagement loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{eng}}$ classifying whether components have mated.
- **Cross-Modal Masked Reconstruction Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{recon}}$)**: Half of the latent dimensions across $[\mathbf{z}^v_t, \mathbf{z}^f_t, \mathbf{p}_t]$ are randomly masked, and the network reconstructs the complete vector from unmasked elements. This ensures vision and force features learn complementary rather than redundant information.

### Policy Learning and Deployment
After pretraining, the encoder is completely frozen. An Actor network receives these representations alongside proprioception to output actions, trained via asymmetric PPO where only the Critic accesses privileged state. Hardware deployment uses identical preprocessing and runs inference directly without updating parameters.

captions.F2: The PACE encoder pipeline. Motion codes are extracted from visual and force temporal buffers via zero-sum kernels, and combined with past proprioception $\mathbf{p}_{t-K}$ to predict future state changes. Backward prediction via time reversal (cycle consistency) is performed simultaneously.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup: Four Demanding Assembly Tasks on Real Hardware
sections.summary: We detail four assembly tasks of varying geometric complexity selected from Factory and AutoMate, along with the real-world evaluation setup using a Franka FR3 robot. Baselines include pose-based PPO with external estimators and end-to-end models.
sections.details:
### Tasks and Environment
Four assembly tasks with diverse geometric demands were evaluated:
- **PegInsert** (Factory): Inserting a 16 mm diameter peg into a hole with ~0.1 mm clearance, testing submillimeter spatial alignment.
- **GearMesh** (Factory): Meshing a 30 mm diameter gear into a stationary gear, requiring lateral adjustments under sustained contact.
- **JointAssemble** (AutoMate): Inserting a rectangular plug, requiring precise alignment in both position and yaw rotation.
- **KnobTighten** (AutoMate): Seating a knob onto a beveled socket, where F/T feedback is critical to sense slip along inclined surfaces.

Hardware evaluations used a Franka FR3 arm equipped with two wrist-mounted RGB cameras ($224\times 224$ pixels) and a 6-axis F/T sensor, operating at 15 Hz. For each task and baseline, 30 consecutive real-world trials were executed with randomized initial and goal poses to strictly assess success rates.

### Baselines
- **Pose-Based PPO**: Standard approach trained with privileged state and deployed using external pose estimation from AprilTags and object detection following IndustReal.
- **No-Pretrain RL**: Reinforcement learning trained directly on DINOv2 features and raw F/T and joint data without encoder pretraining.
- **AugInsert**: Recent baseline using a Perceiver IO architecture with cross-attention fusion, initialized with behavior cloning and fine-tuned via RL.

captions.F3: Real-world experimental setup (left) and the four contact-rich assembly tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, JointAssemble, KnobTighten). Submillimeter assembly is achieved using only two wrist cameras and a wrist F/T sensor.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Outstanding Transfer and Robustness to Perturbations
sections.summary: PACE achieved an average real-world success rate of 93.3% with a sim-to-real drop (Δ) of only 2.7 pp. In feature alignment analyses and severe disturbance tests covering lighting and sensor bias, it decisively outperformed all baselines.
sections.details:
### Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer Performance
In real-world experiments, PACE attained an outstanding average success rate of 93.3% across all four tasks. The performance drop ($\Delta$) from its simulation success rate (96.0%) was merely 2.7 percentage points (pp).

In contrast, Pose-Based PPO achieved near 100% in simulation but dropped to 78.3% on hardware ($\Delta = 18.9$ pp), demonstrating that perception tracking errors are catastrophic for contact tasks. No-Pretrain RL collapsed to 12.5% in reality ($\Delta = 43.7$ pp), and AugInsert reached only 68.3% ($\Delta = 18.4$ pp).

When evaluating cosine similarity of features across identical joint trajectories replayed in simulation and reality, PACE representations maintained high domain consistency even during contact phases: 0.91 for vision and 0.64 for force. Considering raw force data had a similarity of only 0.23, this confirms PACE effectively filters out domain-specific noise.

### Ablation Study
Ablation experiments revealed that removing proprioceptive anchoring ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dyn}}$) caused the sim-to-real drop to surge to 25.5 pp, proving that proprioceptive physical grounding is the primary key to transferability. Dropping the force stream drastically degraded GearMesh and KnobTighten success, while omitting vision caused initial alignment to fail, plunging success rates down to 5–9%.

### Robustness to Real-World Perturbations
On the GearMesh task, systems were tested under four real-world perturbations: extreme illumination changes, 2 cm camera translation shifts, 2 N static F/T sensor bias, and altered background textures. PACE maintained a 90–100% success rate across all conditions. Meanwhile, Pose-Based PPO plummeted to 10% under camera shifts due to pose estimation failures, and AugInsert dropped to 35% under F/T bias.

captions.F4: Cosine similarity profiles between simulation and real-world representations over identical trajectory replays. Compared to raw inputs (gray), PACE features (blue: visual, orange: force) retain high cross-domain similarity even throughout the sustained contact phase.
captions.F5: Hardware perturbation tests on GearMesh. Under severe lighting changes, camera shifts, F/T biases, and background replacements, PACE (dark blue circles) consistently maintains 90–100% success, substantially outperforming baselines.

sections.heading: Discussion: Why Do the Modules Work Synergistically?
sections.summary: We review how anchoring, temporal differencing, masked reconstruction, and multimodal inputs divide labor. We discuss the general principle of using a dependable sensor as an anchor to structure representations for less reliable modalities.
sections.details:
The results highlight how each component of PACE acts in close synergy:
- **Proprioception Anchoring**: The central driver bridging the sim-to-real gap, tying latent features directly to underlying physical motion.
- **Zero-Sum Temporal Difference Kernels**: Instantly cancel hardware manufacturing variations, thermal F/T sensor drift, and inconsistent scene lighting.
- **Masked Reconstruction**: Prevents inter-modality redundancy and strengthens robustness, allowing force feedback to compensate when vision suffers from shadows or occlusion, and vision to guide policy prior to contact.
- **Vision-Force Coordination**: Accurately reflects the complementary nature of assembly, where vision is required for coarse approach and force is indispensable for fine insertion and friction mitigation.

This paradigm—supervising high-shift modalities (vision and force) using a low-shift, domain-consistent sensor (proprioception)—offers a versatile blueprint extending beyond assembly to broader robotic manipulation and mobile robot sim-to-real transfer.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: By pretraining encoders anchored to proprioception, PACE reaches remarkable assembly accuracy without real-world data or external pose tracking. It stands as a milestone demonstrating how stable modalities can regularize others for robust transfer.
sections.details:
This paper presented PACE, a pretraining encoder framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for contact-rich assembly tasks. Evaluated on four demanding tasks from Factory and AutoMate, it achieved an average real-world success rate of 93.3% with only a 2.7-percentage-point degradation from simulation, operating entirely without real-world fine-tuning or external object pose tracking.

Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of physical dynamics regularization via proprioception anchoring, offset cancellation through zero-sum differencing, and complementary representation learning via masked reconstruction. For robot learning facing persistent simulation-to-reality disparities, this work demonstrates the immense value of anchored multimodal representation pretraining.

takeaways: The most powerful tool for Sim-to-Real transfer is anchoring representation learning to the modality that exhibits the least reality gap: proprioception.
Applying zero-sum temporal difference kernels to convolutions mathematically cancels out lighting variations and force sensor offset drifts.
Systems dependent on external object pose estimation collapse under millimeter-level errors; learning robust end-to-end representations offers superior reliability for contact-rich tasks.
Coarse approaches require vision while insertions demand force; masked autoencoding effectively exposes and leverages the complementary strengths of both modalities.
limitations: Requires pre-training an expert policy with privileged simulation state to collect demonstration trajectories, assuming the target task can be modeled accurately in a simulator.
Requires manual pre-tuning of shared hardware configurations, such as impedance controller gains and wrist camera mounting positions.

Evaluated on a 4-DoF operational space (3D translation + yaw) with roll and pitch fixed vertically; extending the framework to full 6-DoF spatial rotations for complex 3D assemblies remains future work.
